[b]The Friends of Liberty[/b]

A new treatise has been mysteriously disseminated in Thrysmoran social media sites, political forums, and in pamphlets distributed by unknown individuals claiming to be the [i]Amigos da Liberdade[/i] or "Friends of Liberty". The treatise, seemingly a social democratic text, would be authored by a certain pseudonymous [i]Muramullo[/i], roughly meaning "they who whisper through walls", and would be clearly a critique of Thrysmora's current government policies and their potential contributions to the rising power of communism everywhere. Attached below is the full essay as was seen on a pamphlet removed by a God-fearing citizen:

[spoiler=Why communism?]

[list]

[b]Why communism?, by Muramullo[/b]

Why is it that even now, two centuries after the Elseyran continent firmly decreed that all men are created equal, with rights and dignities that were to be accorded to them by the rule of law, there are still those disenfranchised and devoid of all hope for liberal democracy? Why is it that, even after two centuries of failed extremist movements seizing democratic movement to instigate their revolutionary perception of utopia, there are still those in the depths of existence who continue to strive beneath the banner of the red flag?

Well, why not?

To the oblivious eye, it is unthinkable to even consider such a premise. A one-party state, a single legitimate political line, opaque councils and commissions, an ever-present police force, the disappearance of dissent, show trials and kangaroo courts, the surrender of private property. Those who live in their humble homes know nothing of the cause of left extremism and so deride it as malicious and poisonous to the spirit of liberty and nationality. 

Yet, the conscious eye wonders why it has not happened more often.

Before sociology understood the conflict among the classes, the prevailing view that permeated all human history was that the frameworks that held up these great kingdoms and empires were built on a series of structures each with their own independent functions, generating both intended and unintended consequences that lead those structures toward equilibrium.

Suppose one might ask of how the Qianxun monarchy worked, under this framework you think of the Emperor who ruled as the Son of Heaven, then his kindly eunuchs and military generals, his concubines, and other offices of the court each with their own customary and executive functions. Then we discuss the secretariats, the departments, the ministries as the legislative and consultative power of the monarchy, staffed with scholar-bureaucrats of the imperial examinations through which the wisest of Qianxun were funnelled. Then soldiers, merchants, monks, peasants.

Every component of the structure had its purpose or function, like the appendages and organs that made up the human body, and the descecration of one or more of these components taint the system and forces it to correct itself until it could again reach equilibrium. 

Kingdoms and empires, therefore, fell because too many of its components had gone astray. Disloyal generals, scheming wives, hungry peasants, failing harvests, changing climate, all of which would prevent the components from appropriately administering their intended roles. As the structure contorts into indecipherable shapes or is destroyed, human society persists still until the distortion could be reformed into a new and functional equilibrium.

This way of thinking persists as the teleology of all Thrysmoran political theory.

According to its leaders, all classes and all institutions have a basis and a function, a dutiful commitment to the whole. Educated professionals have their place in the system, as do great leaders and wealthy men, who spend more and help contribute to an ever-specializing economy. However, together with the wealthy are the weak and frail, poor and starving, oppressed and forgotten. What is their purpose in the structure? What are their functions, so grand and legitimate and important, that they must remain as organs of the whole?

The Thrysmorans say that these men are good in the station of life that they were born in and that their happiness may be found through collaboration with their benevolent masters. To perceive the world in structures and functions, therefore, is to perceive the world as a just and rational order, when it is not. 

What exists now is not due to mankind's rational approach towards equilibrium but because of conflict. This world we live in is a field of conflict between good and bad, rich and poor, those with arms and those who do not, the victorious and the defeated. All conflict is based on the capture of resources in a finite existence. And so, the underlying frameworks of our existence are also organized according to conflict. Those who are empowered exist because they have triumphed over those who do not, and generations thence receive the fruits of that triumph for its own means.

In the Kingdom of Thrysmora, the issue of conflict has been resolved not through a rebellion of its fundamental inequalities but through its total acceptance.

Facendas, plantations, landlords, corporations, and government institutions continue to remain the dominant agricultural force in the country in the face of overwhelming peasant landlessness. Structural functionalists will say that these institutions exist because they are efficient and supplant the unnecessary subsistence agricultural practices of the commons, even as these monopolistic cartels raise prices, destroy unions, and watch quietly as the families ruined by their land seizures are left to starve and rot in an early grave. All that glitters is not gold.

So, if all things are derived from conflict and not function, then what drives conflict? On Erene, three main factors drive tension: The economy, the environment, and human society. 

Economically, the Kingdom of Thrysmora is a developed country, with decent industrialization and manufacturing sectors, a respectable class of working professionals, good education, and generous incentives to those seeking to bring innovation to its structure. Conversely, it is chauvinistic, opportunistic, exploitative, negligient of the externalities that destroy the world around it for profit, unconscious, and beset by a desirous avarice for growth itself. 

Environmentally, Thrysmora is the Pearl of the White Straits, nestled deep into its waters, facing Elseyr, with rolling hills and beautiful greenlands, ample fauna, good air, and moderate temperatures. Conversely, many of these things have since been lost to time, entire forests bulldozed, roots uprooted and soil loosened in the quest for industry. Where natural disasters might lash out to punish Thrysmoran impunity, it responds with grey infrastructure to rebel against nature, destroying nature further in a vicious cycle. 

Socially, the Thrysmoran worker today lives a life of luxury compared to the worker of the last century. He is literate, conscious of politics, with an understanding of the nature of the world, attuned to the news, with internet access, and ample funds to pursue his own hobbies. Conversely, he was born and has lived in the same echelon of human society since his birth, he labors and earns minimally, he loves to think but has not thought to love, fears the costs of parenthood, and thinks little of self-actualization when modesty alone demands of him such great trials. At any moment, ill-health and disaster will make him come undone.

All the world is struggle and conflict. Between the environmentalist and the economist is conflict over natural resources. Between the economist and the sociologist is conflict over equity and land use. Between the sociologist and the environmentalist is conflict over the necessity of development.

In the realm of conflict, orders is manifest not because it must but because in that head-long struggle shall there be one side that triumphs over the other. 

For Thrysmorans, bloody victory has been the fact of life. Corporations expelling families from centuries-old land, student protesters stared down by heavily armed policemen, an elderly man left to die outside the hospital he could not afford, a lone child wailing in the community graveyard. The cycle then repeats again, and darkens as the greedy become more audacious.

In the Kaiserreich, student protesters are ziptied and thrown into black vans, an elderly man is beaten mercilessly after holding up a placard of protest, the corpse of a child rotting on the pavement after trying to protect that man, a starving dog feasting on the remains after being abandoned by his master. The cycle repeats again, and darkens still.

The Vespurians know to conceal their evil. Students merely disappear without ever being seen again, and men do not grow old. The streets glow radiantly to remind the commons of the beauty of this liberal democracy, while agitators are mocked and personified as fools. The cycle repeats again, and in that great darkness is the heart of all these triumphs against conflict.

In the heart of darkness is a despair so poignant and so inflamed that the dregs of all existence is empowered by the yielding to the singular course of action: Revolt.

Why communism?

Because in all societies will be those that receive less than most. In a cruel and meaningless world in which men still strive to find filaments of good, people turn to the red flag because it seems to them the way out of their terrible plight.

What happens when the revolution has succeeded? In all successful revolutions have been the drunkenness of victory, the all-pervasive need to instigate the immediate consequences of the enemy's destruction at the expense of the years of careful praxis before. Even when the dictatorship of the proletariat is instituted, what then happens? The evils of the old have been eradicated, yet the world remains finite, resources remain finite, the people continue to need and strive and want.

The purpose of a communist society is to eradicate the perceived imbalanced created by capitalist society and to enrich in the human race the supposition of its innate duty to the common good. But what must be sacrificed in order for this deterministic future to be assured? It is as I've said. A one-party state, a single legitimate political line, opaque councils and commissions, the disappearance of dissent, show trials and kangaroo courts, the surrender of private property.

"Why must I concern myself with these things?" a comrade-in-arms might opine, "when I've little enjoined them when I was free?"

And so, these things which they once called the "rights of man" are surrendered to the party. State entities seize land from the corporations to give to the poor, student protesters are placated, and the weak and old are guaranteed their social benefits as the means of production transition from the profit motive to the social motive. The revolutionaries hold their breathe. Has the cycle been broken?

However, a revolution does not liberate men from scarcity. Scarcity can't come any sooner. The three conflicts are economic, environmental, social. The mere destruction of the old does not replace the needs of the many that must be paid for at someone's expense.

In the drunkenness of victory, the people seem to ignore the formation of the all-powerful politburo, the secret police force to ensure orthodoxy and orthopraxy in the new communist order, the land seizures not for profit but for state profit, the central planning, the ominous new party slogans. In the morning the revolutionary wakes but realizes that the darkness of the world had not lightened still. Student protesters are shot as they rally for an end to collectivization, an elderly man is butchered in an interrogation room as his child and all later generations are dispersed from the earth, a dog lays down by his fallen master's grave and closes his eyes for the last time. The world darkens, the cycle repeats.

Why communism?

Because all the world is conflict and men find satisfaction in victory, but glory and triumph are short-sighted when done to overwhelm and destroy the workings of the old. But the starving and the dying do not concern themselves with these grandiose issues. Will a starving man concern himself with the mold of a slice of bread? Deprived of all things, man will seek comforts in the way of beasts. If the nations of Erene seek to prevent the descent of their respective nations into communistic indulgence, then do not let it these things happen.

[/list]
